name: Numbami
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Numbami is not in the catalog. All three works with stress in the title (Cinque 1993; Kruger 2023; Gargiulo et al. 2019) are 'null'-keyword misattachments in Glottolog and concern other languages; none bears on Numbami. this search of works with stress in the title found the real sources: Bradshaw's 2025 grammar (UH Press; Phonology ch. pp. 17-31, DOI 10.2307/jj.22362172.6 / 10.1515/9798880702213-004) is the best candidate but is paywalled and bot-walled everywhere (JSTOR, De Gruyter, MUSE, Google Books; Unpaywall not OA); Bradshaw 2006 (OL 45) is closed; Bradshaw 1982 dissertation is on ScholarSpace but restricted to UH login. Openly read: Bradshaw's 2014 Numbami-English/English-Numbami dictionaries (no stress rule; only 'stressed/accented' tags on clitics), Bradshaw 1978 Kivung article (scanned; no stress statement), Ransdell-Green 2022 Kala thesis (no Numbami stress), and the Wikipedia article authored by Bradshaw, whose Ideophones section marks word stress with acute accents on ten forms (bái-andala, golópu-adala, paká-adala, pilipíli-adala, tíki-adala..) without a general rule. classification: no explicit word-stress rule for Numbami is openly available; acquire Bradshaw 2025 ch. 3 (high) and Bradshaw 2006 (high).

earlier_scan.source_named: Bradshaw, Joel. 2006. Grammatically marked ideophones in Numbami and Jabêm. Oceanic Linguistics 45:53-63 (marks Numbami word stress with acute accents); also Bradshaw 1982 UH PhD dissertation. Neither openly online.

new_statements.quote: In the following examples, acute accents show the placement of word stress. bái-andala 'overcast, clouded over'; dendende-ándala 'shivering'; golópu-adala 'slipping or dripping through'; kí-andala 'scorching, parched'; paká-adala 'getting light, flashing on, popping'; pilipíli-adala 'flapping, fluttering'; sí-andala 'shooting up, springing away'; sulúku-adala 'sucking, slurping'; taká-adala 'stuck fast, planted firmly'; tíki-adala 'going dark'
new_statements.citation: Bradshaw, Joel. 'Numbami language', Wikipedia, section 'Ideophones' (text added by Bradshaw himself in the revision of, summarizing Bradshaw 2006, Oceanic Linguistics 45:53-63)
new_statements.locator: Wikipedia 'Numbami language', section Ideophones (current text = 2007-02-20 revision by user Joel Bradshaw)
new_statements.reading: First-hand (the documenter's own text) but not a rule: it only marks stress on ten ideophones. Stress sits on the ideophone base, not on the suffix -a(n)dala: penult of the base in golópu, pilipíli, sulúku, tíki; final syllable in paká, taká; monosyllabic bases bái, kí, sí; and on the suffix's first syllable after the reduplicated base dendende. No general word-stress rule for ordinary Numbami words is stated anywhere in the open sources read (dictionaries, Kivung 1978, Kala thesis). The rule, if any, should be in Bradshaw 2025 ch. 3 Phonology (pp. 17-31) or Bradshaw 2006/1982, none openly accessible.

sources.quote: te1 n encl Topic marker E te, e imungga. Him, he went first. Woya te wambilalo. Me, I don't know. [never stressed] ... te3 pron one Te, tikamba tinggo ka buli. One, they call buli. [of a known set, stressed]
sources.note: No orthography or stress note in the front matter; the only stress remarks are usage tags on function words: 'te1 n encl Topic marker.. [never stressed]', 'te3 pron one.. [of a known set, stressed]', 'manu.. [never accented]', 'manu? Which one is it? [always accented]'.

sources.quote: Words like kopi 'coffee', suga 'sugar', or sege 'saw' already fit the Numbami preference for open syllables.
